title: Attacking the sawtooth: the tile predicts the cost, but B does not predict the tile

schedule.note: two independent runs, 13 + 12 odd batches, every one width 1 so the width axis is frozen

prereg.rule: for odd B: B mod 8 in {5,7} -> heavy tile_B = 8; {1,3} -> tile_B = 4
prereg.falsifier: any disagreement among the 12 kills it
prereg.why: B=141 and B=143 took tile_B=16 and B=153 took tile_B=32, values the rule does not contemplate. Across 25 batch sizes Triton used tile_B in {4, 8, 16, 32, 123, 127}, so no residue of B can select it.

mechanism_confirmed.test: mean absolute cost jump between neighbouring batches, split by whether the tile signature changed
mechanism_confirmed.verdict: replicated: jumps are 3.4x and 4.6x larger when the tile changes

the_usable_result.finding: The full tile signature groups the cost tightly, and the cheapest signature is separable. Across both runs the signature '8,1,8,8,3|8,1,8,8,3' has n=6 with max 0.007950, while the next signature '4,1,8,16,3|8,1,8,8,3' has n=6 with min 0.007977: no overlap.
the_usable_result.the_procedure: Since the tile is not predictable but IS visible at compile time, select the batch size by COMPILING the candidates and reading the tile signature out of the HLO backend_config, then pick the cheap signature. A compile is about 40 s and needs no simulation, against a full production run of 10 to 12 min per candidate.

honest_limits: The no-overlap margin is only 0.3% with n=6 on each side; another sample could overlap. This is a usable selector, not a proven law.
Within the cheap signature there is still 3.2% spread (0.007702 to 0.007950), unexplained.

RESOLVED: the production pair B=151 against B=153 measured +15.0% at 4,000,000 sweeps against +12.2% predicted from 3600, so the effect survives and grows. The earlier worry came from the 65/75 pair, whose 5.7% gap was inside the noise band; this one is not.
The signature set is a property of this jaxlib/XLA build and may move with a version bump.

The production validation is ONE pair, a single run each, no repeats. It establishes that a 12% short-cell gap survives; it does not establish the survival of the 0.3% no-overlap margin between adjacent signatures.

production_validation.why_this_pair: the largest gap available at 3600 sweeps, 12.2%, so the one most likely to clear the +-2.5% extrapolation noise
production_validation.extrapolation_error: short cells UNDER-reported by 2.7 percentage points
production_validation.verdict: THE SELECTOR SURVIVES PRODUCTION, and the gap GREW. 12.2% at 3600 sweeps became 15.0% at 4,000,000. Choosing the cheap tile signature saves 1.268 s per replica, which is 13.0% of what the dear one costs.
production_validation.resolution_threshold_confirmed: This settles the pattern. The 65/75 pair was 5.7% on short cells and 0.6% at production: it died, because 5.7% sits inside the +-2.5%-per-point noise band. This pair was 12.2% and became 15.0%: it survived, because it is far outside. So the working rule is that short-cell features above roughly 5% are real and features below it are not resolvable.
production_validation.per_kernel_note: The common kernels (the rolls, the reductions) move only 1 to 3% between the two. The difference sits in the Triton fusions, which appear under different generated names in each build (fusion_1364/1362 at B=151, fusion_1474/1473 at B=153). Precise per-kernel attribution is NOT claimed here, because name-matched deltas already misled us once in this work.

payoff.wall_clock: 21.3 min against 24.9 min for this pair
payoff.cost_of_finding_it: about 40 s of compilation per candidate, no simulation
